Nandini's laptop fan whirred in the small computer lab of the polytechnic in Kasba. Her program to sort marks kept crashing on line twelve. She wanted to ask the tool for the finished code, but stopped: if I get it now, I won't know why it broke.

So she stared at the error for ten minutes, tried changing the loop twice, and failed. Only then did she paste the error and her attempt and ask, "Explain what this message means. Don't write the solution." The tool said she was mixing text and numbers. "Now ask me three questions about that so I know I've got it," she typed.

Gopika, at the next desk, saw her fix it and asked, "How?" Nandini grinned. "I tried first, then it taught me."

qa.q: On which line did Nandini's program keep crashing?
Why did Nandini decide to stare at the error before asking the tool?
qa.a: Nandini feared that receiving finished code would leave her not knowing why it broke, so she wanted to keep her own thinking active.

qa.q: What could Nandini do if the tool's explanation still confused her, and why?
qa.a: Nandini could ask Gopika at the next desk to walk through the error with her, because a person can see what she already understands.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel after seeing Nandini fix the crash?
qa.a: Gopika may feel curious and a little encouraged, wanting to try the same try-first method on Gopika's own program.

grounding: The student attempts a coding problem first, then asks the tool to explain the error and quiz her on the concept.

subtype: Approach: use the tool as a tutor with own attempt first [Thinking]
passage:
Montevideo, a rainy Tuesday. Mina sat in the university's student lounge with her programming assignment: a function that should count the vowels in a word, but kept returning one too many.
Santiago, beside her, was already typing the whole problem into a chatbot. "Done in a minute."
"I want to try first," Mina said. She spent twenty minutes printing values after each loop. The extra count showed up at the end of every word, but she couldn't see why.
Then she opened the tool and wrote: "Don't fix my code. Explain what might cause an off-by-one error in this loop." It pointed to her range going one step past the last letter. She groaned, fixed it herself, then asked: "Now give me three quick questions on loop ranges." She got two right.
"I'll remember this one," she told Santiago. "I fought it first."

qa.q: What was Mina's function supposed to count?
qa.a: It was supposed to count the vowels in a word.

qa.q: Why did Mina want to try first, and how did she feel when the tool pointed to the bug?
qa.a: She wanted the thinking to be her own; when the tool showed her range went one step too far, she groaned, a mix of frustration and relief.

qa.q: What else could Mina do with the tool after the quiz?
qa.a: She could ask it to explain the one question she got wrong, then write a small new loop herself to test that she really understands it.

qa.q: How might Santiago see Mina's approach?
qa.a: Santiago may think she wasted twenty minutes, but her line about fighting it first could make him wonder whether his quick answer will stick.

grounding: Shows a student attempting a coding problem first, then asking the tool to explain the error and quiz them, so the learning sticks.

The computer lab closed at six, and it was already five fifteen. Kishore's database query kept returning every order twice.
Pankaj, the lab assistant, was locking cupboards. "Want the chatbot to just rewrite it?"
"Not yet." Kishore talked through it aloud. "Two tables, joined on customer ID. Each customer can have two addresses. So each order matches twice. Is that it?" He added a filter for the main address. Still duplicates, fewer now.
Then he opened the tool and typed: "I think my join is matching too many rows. Explain why, but don't write the query." It explained that one table had a duplicate customer row. He found it, removed it, and the numbers came right. Then he asked, "Quiz me on joins, three questions." He missed one and asked why.
At five fifty-five Pankaj switched off the lights behind him.

qa.q: What was wrong with Kishore's query at first?
qa.a: It kept returning every order twice.

qa.q: How can you tell Kishore wanted to understand the problem, not just fix it?
qa.a: He felt determined to reason it out himself, talking through the tables aloud and asking the tool to explain but not write the query.

qa.q: What else could Kishore try next time before reaching for the tool?
qa.a: He could check each table for duplicate rows first, since a quick count of customer IDs would have shown the extra row sooner.

qa.q: How might Pankaj see Kishore's approach as the lab was closing?
qa.a: Pankaj might have been a little impatient to lock up, but also noticed that Kishore refused a quick rewrite and worked it out.

grounding: Shows a student attempting the problem first, then using the tool to explain the error and quiz them, keeping the thinking active.
